title: Ἀχιλλέως ὁρμὴ καὶ Ἶρις
titleEn: Achilles’ Resolve and the Message of Iris — Iliad 18.97–201
part: Achilles’ Resolve and the Message of Iris (18.97–201)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Achilles answers his mother. He wishes he had died before failing Patroclus, curses the anger that Agamemnon roused in him, and says he will go to kill Hector and accept his own death afterwards, since even Heracles did not escape his fate. Thetis agrees that it is right to defend his comrades, but tells him not to enter the fight until she brings new armour from Hephaestus at dawn, since Hector wears his old armour. She tells her sister Nereids to go home to their father, and herself goes to Olympus. On the field the Achaeans flee to the ships, and Hector, three times repulsed by the two Ajaxes, still tries to drag Patroclus off, until Iris, sent secretly by Hera, tells Achilles to rise. He has no armour, but she bids him show himself unarmed at the ditch to frighten the Trojans.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: And her, greatly vexed, addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, Achilles, swift of foot, said to her:
sentences.n: This is the narrator’s line, and it answers the end of Thetis’ speech in the previous part, where she told Achilles that his own death would follow Hector’s. τὴν is Thetis, ‘her’. μέγα is the adverb ‘greatly’, and ὀχθήσας ‘vexed, troubled’ is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω. The epithet πόδας ὠκύς, ‘swift in feet’, is translated every time, as at 1.84.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα τεθναίην, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον ἑταίρῳ
κτεινομένῳ ἐπαμῦναι· ὃ μὲν μάλα τηλόθι πάτρης
ἔφθιτ’, ἐμεῖο δὲ δῆσεν ἀρῆς ἀλκτῆρα γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autika tethnaiēn, epei ouk ar’ emellon hetairōi
kteinomenōi epamynai· ho men mala tēlothi patrēs
ephthit’, emeio de dēsen arēs alktēra genesthai.
sentences.l:
“May I die at once, since I was not, it seems, to come to the defence of my companion
as he was being killed; he, far from his fatherland,
perished, and had need of me to become a warder-off of ruin.
sentences.i: “May I die this instant, since I was not, it seems, to come to my companion’s defence as he was killed. He perished far from his fatherland, and he needed me to ward off ruin from him.
sentences.n: Achilles’ speech begins with a wish, and the optative τεθναίην means ‘may I be dead’. ἄρ’ marks a fact that has just dawned on him, hence ‘it seems’. ἐπαμῦναι is an aorist infinitive, ‘to come to the defence of’, taking the dative ἑταίρῳ. δῆσεν is a Homeric aorist of δέω ‘lack, need’ and takes the genitive ἐμεῖο, ‘had need of me’. ἀρῆς is ‘ruin, harm’, and ἀλκτῆρα ‘warder-off’ names the helper who should have come.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ οὐ νέομαί γε φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
οὐδέ τι Πατρόκλῳ γενόμην φάος οὐδ’ ἑτάροισι
τοῖς ἄλλοις, οἳ δὴ πολέες δάμεν Ἕκτορι δίῳ,
ἀλλ’ ἧμαι παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης,
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ epei ou neomai ge philēn es patrida gaian,
oude ti Patroklōi genomēn phaos oud’ hetaroisi
tois allois, hoi dē polees damen Hektori diōi,
all’ hēmai para nēusin etōsion achthos arourēs,
sentences.l:
But now, since I am not returning to my dear native land,
nor have I become a light to Patroclus nor to my other
companions, who in great numbers were subdued by Hector, the heavenly,
but sit by the ships, a useless burden of the plough-land,
sentences.i: But now, since I am not going home to my dear native land, and have been no light to Patroclus or to the rest of my companions, the many who were overcome by heavenly Hector, but sit by the ships, a useless burden on the plough-land,
sentences.n: A long sentence of reasons that is not completed until the wish at line 107. νέομαι is present in form but looks ahead, ‘I am not going to return’. γενόμην is an aorist without the augment, ‘I became’; to be ‘a light’ (φάος) is to be a rescue and a saving presence. δάμεν is the aorist passive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’. ἄχθος ἀρούρης, ‘a burden of the plough-land’, is a phrase the Odyssey also uses of a useless man; ἐτώσιον is ‘useless, to no purpose’.

sentences.t:
τοῖος ἐὼν οἷος οὔ τις Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
ἐν πολέμῳ· ἀγορῇ δέ τ’ ἀμείνονές εἰσι καὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr:
toios eōn hoios ou tis Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn
en polemōi· agorēi de t’ ameinones eisi kai alloi.
sentences.l:
being such as no other of the bronze-shirted Achaeans is
in war; but in assembly there are others too who are better.
sentences.i: though in war I am such as no other of the bronze-shirted Achaeans is, in assembly there are others too who are better.
sentences.n: τοῖος ἐὼν οἷος οὔ τις … is ‘being of such a kind as no one …’, and it sums up the contrast of the previous lines: the best in war, yet idle. The stock epithet χαλκοχιτώνων is ‘bronze-shirted’, translated every time. ἀγορῇ is a dative of respect, ‘in assembly’, and ἀμείνονες is the comparative of ἀγαθός. The particle τε in ἀγορῇ δέ τ’ is the general-truth τε; Achilles admits that others speak better.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἔρις ἔκ τε θεῶν ἔκ τ’ ἀνθρώπων ἀπόλοιτο
καὶ χόλος, ὅς τ’ ἐφέηκε πολύφρονά περ χαλεπῆναι,
ὅς τε πολὺ γλυκίων μέλιτος καταλειβομένοιο
ἀνδρῶν ἐν στήθεσσιν ἀέξεται ἠΰτε καπνός·
sentences.tr:
hōs eris ek te theōn ek t’ anthrōpōn apoloito
kai cholos, hos t’ epheēke polyphrona per chalepēnai,
hos te poly glykiōn melitos kataleibomenoio
andrōn en stēthessin aexetai ēÿte kapnos·
sentences.l:
Would that strife were destroyed from among gods and from among men,
and anger, which drives even a man of many counsels to be angry,
which, much sweeter than honey as it drips down,
in the breasts of men grows like smoke;
sentences.i: If only strife would perish from among gods and men, and anger too, which drives even a man of many counsels to rage, and which, much sweeter than honey as it drips down, grows in the breasts of men like smoke;
sentences.n: ἀπόλοιτο is an optative of wish, ‘would that it perish’. ἔρις is ‘strife’ and χόλος ‘anger’, which are different words. ἐφέηκε is an aorist of ἐφίημι ‘set on, drive’, here stating what anger always does, and χαλεπῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of χαλεπαίνω ‘be harsh, be angry’. πολύφρων is ‘of many counsels’. ἀέξεται is the passive of ἀέξω ‘make grow’, so anger ‘grows’. καταλειβομένοιο is ‘dripping down’, said of honey.

sentences.t: ὡς ἐμὲ νῦν ἐχόλωσεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων.
sentences.tr: hōs eme nyn echolōsen anax andrōn Agamemnōn.
sentences.l: so now has the lord of men, Agamemnon, made me angry.
sentences.i: in just that way has Agamemnon, lord of men, now made me angry.
sentences.n: ὡς picks up the whole of the wish and the comparison before it: that is how anger grows, and that is how Agamemnon has made me angry. ἐχόλωσεν is the aorist of χολόω, ‘make angry’, from the same root as χόλος. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν, ‘lord of men’, is the stock title of Agamemnon and keeps its fixed English.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν προτετύχθαι ἐάσομεν ἀχνύμενοί περ,
θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλον δαμάσαντες ἀνάγκῃ·
sentences.tr:
alla ta men protetychthai easomen achnymenoi per,
thymon eni stēthessi philon damasantes anankēi·
sentences.l:
But those things, done now and past, we will let be, though we grieve,
having subdued the dear heart in our breasts by necessity;
sentences.i: But what is done and past we will let be, grieving though we are, mastering the heart in our breasts by necessity;
sentences.n: προτετύχθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of προτεύχω, ‘to have been done before’, so τὰ μὲν προτετύχθαι is ‘the things already done’. ἐάσομεν is a future, ‘we will let be’, and the plural is Achilles speaking of himself; ἀχνύμενοί περ is ‘grieving though we are’. δαμάσαντες is the aorist participle of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, and ἀνάγκῃ ‘by necessity’ is a dative of means. Achilles gives up his anger against Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ εἶμ’ ὄφρα φίλης κεφαλῆς ὀλετῆρα κιχείω
Ἕκτορα·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ eim’ ophra philēs kephalēs oletēra kicheiō
Hektora·
sentences.l:
but now I go, so that the destroyer of my dear head I may find,
Hector;
sentences.i: but now I go, to find the destroyer of the one so dear to me, Hector;
sentences.n: ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive κιχείω gives purpose, ‘so that I may find’. κεφαλή ‘head’ stands for the person, as often, so φίλης κεφαλῆς ὀλετῆρα is ‘the destroyer of the dear one’; the English of i spells that out and l keeps ‘head’. ὀλετῆρα is a noun of agent from ὄλλυμι. The name Ἕκτορα is held back to the start of the next line, and a pause follows it.

sentences.t:
κῆρα δ’ ἐγὼ τότε δέξομαι ὁππότε κεν δὴ
Ζεὺς ἐθέλῃ τελέσαι ἠδ’ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr:
kēra d’ egō tote dexomai hoppote ken dē
Zeus ethelēi telesai ēd’ athanatoi theoi alloi.
sentences.l:
and the death-fate I will then accept, whenever
Zeus wishes to bring it about, and the other immortal gods.
sentences.i: and I shall accept my fated death whenever Zeus wishes to bring it about, and the other immortal gods.
sentences.n: κήρ, accusative κῆρα, is the death-fate, the power that brings a man’s death; in i it is ‘fated death’. δέξομαι is a future, ‘I will receive’, and ὁππότε κεν with the subjunctive ἐθέλῃ is ‘whenever’. Zeus is named first, and the other gods are added after him. Achilles has already been told by Thetis that his death follows Hector’s, so this is acceptance, not a new decision.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ βίη Ἡρακλῆος φύγε κῆρα,
ὅς περ φίλτατος ἔσκε Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr:
oude gar oude biē Hēraklēos phyge kēra,
hos per philtatos eske Dii Kroniōni anakti·
sentences.l:
For not even the might of Heracles escaped the death-fate,
he who indeed was dearest of all to Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord;
sentences.i: For not even the might of Heracles escaped his death, though he was dearest of all to lord Zeus, the son of Cronus;
sentences.n: Achilles gives a precedent: even Heracles died. βίη Ἡρακλῆος, ‘the might of Heracles’, is a periphrasis for the hero himself. ὅς περ is ‘he who indeed’, and i turns it into ‘though’ because the point is that even a favourite died; ἔσκε is an iterative past, ‘used to be’, hence ‘was dearest’. φίλτατος is the superlative of φίλος, and Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι is ‘lord Zeus, the son of Cronus’, using the epithet as it stands elsewhere.

sentences.t: ἀλλά ἑ μοῖρα δάμασσε καὶ ἀργαλέος χόλος Ἥρης.
sentences.tr: alla he moira damasse kai argaleos cholos Hērēs.
sentences.l: but fate subdued him, and the grievous anger of Hera.
sentences.i: no, fate overcame him, and the grievous anger of Hera.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ἑ is ἀλλά ‘but’ and ἑ ‘him’, written as two words. δάμασσε is an aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, with two subjects, μοῖρα ‘fate’ and χόλος ‘anger’. ἀργαλέος is ‘grievous, hard to bear’. The Iliad often mentions Hera’s hatred of Heracles, and here it is simply given as a cause of his death.

sentences.t:
ὣς καὶ ἐγών, εἰ δή μοι ὁμοίη μοῖρα τέτυκται,
κείσομ’ ἐπεί κε θάνω·
sentences.tr:
hōs kai egōn, ei dē moi homoiē moira tetyktai,
keisom’ epei ke thanō·
sentences.l:
So I too, if a like fate has been fashioned for me,
shall lie still when I am dead;
sentences.i: So I too, if a similar fate has been fashioned for me, shall lie still once I am dead;
sentences.n: ὣς καὶ ἐγών is ‘so I also’, answering the example of Heracles. ὁμοίη is ‘like’, and τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘has been made’. κείσομ’ is the future of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, and ἐπεί κε θάνω is ‘when I have died’, an aorist subjunctive with κε. Pause at the ano teleia, mid-line.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἀροίμην,
καί τινα Τρωϊάδων καὶ Δαρδανίδων βαθυκόλπων
ἀμφοτέρῃσιν χερσὶ παρειάων ἁπαλάων
δάκρυ’ ὀμορξαμένην ἁδινὸν στοναχῆσαι ἐφείην,
sentences.tr:
nyn de kleos esthlon aroimēn,
kai tina Trōïadōn kai Dardanidōn bathykolpōn
amphoterēisin chersi pareiaōn hapalaōn
dakry’ omorxamenēn hadinon stonachēsai epheiēn,
sentences.l:
but now may I win noble glory,
and may I make some one of the Trojan women and of the deep-bosomed Dardanian women
with both hands from her tender cheeks
having wiped the tear, heavily to groan aloud,
sentences.i: but now may I win noble glory, and may I make some one of the Trojan women and the deep-bosomed Dardanian women wipe the tears from her tender cheeks with both hands and groan heavily,
sentences.n: Both ἀροίμην and ἐφείην are aorist optatives of wish, ‘may I win’ and ‘may I set (her) to’. ἐφείην is from ἐφίημι and takes the infinitive στοναχῆσαι ‘to groan aloud’. Τρωϊάδων are Trojan women and Δαρδανίδων Dardanian, that is also Trojan, women. βαθυκόλπων ‘deep-bosomed’ is a stock epithet for them, κόλπος being the deep fold of the dress over the breast. ὀμορξαμένην is an aorist middle participle, ‘having wiped’; ἁδινόν is the adverb of ἁδινός ‘thick, thronging’, here ‘heavily’, and is taken with the groaning.

sentences.t: γνοῖεν δ’ ὡς δὴ δηρὸν ἐγὼ πολέμοιο πέπαυμαι·
sentences.tr: gnoien d’ hōs dē dēron egō polemoio pepaumai·
sentences.l: and let them know that for a long time now I have ceased from war;
sentences.i: and let them learn that I have stayed out of the fighting for a long time now;
sentences.n: γνοῖεν is an aorist optative of γιγνώσκω, ‘may they know’, still part of the wish begun at ἐφείην. δηρόν is ‘for a long time’, and πέπαυμαι is the perfect middle of παύω, ‘I have ceased, I have rested’. The wish is for fame won at the Trojans’ expense, and the weeping women are the proof of it.

sentences.t: μὴ δέ μ’ ἔρυκε μάχης φιλέουσά περ· οὐδέ με πείσεις.
sentences.tr: mē de m’ eryke machēs phileousa per· oude me peiseis.
sentences.l: and do not hold me back from the fight, loving me though you do; and you will not persuade me.”
sentences.i: And do not hold me back from battle, loving me as you do; you will not persuade me.”
sentences.n: μή with the imperative ἔρυκε is ‘do not hold back’. ἔρυκε is the imperative of ἐρύκω, and μάχης is a genitive of separation, ‘from the fight’. φιλέουσά περ is a concessive participle, ‘though you love me’. οὐδέ με πείσεις is a flat future, ‘and you will not persuade me’. The words μὴ δέ are printed as two. The speech ends here; Thetis’ reply is the next speech, introduced by a paragraph break.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita thea Thetis argyropeza·
sentences.l: Him then answered the goddess Thetis, silver-footed:
sentences.i: Then the goddess Thetis, silver-footed, answered him:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula, with the epithet ἀργυρόπεζα ‘silver-footed’ that the poem gives Thetis and that is translated every time. τὸν is Achilles, ‘him’, and the verb ἠμείβετο is an imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. θεά ‘goddess’ stands before the name. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t:
ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε τέκνον ἐτήτυμον οὐ κακόν ἐστι
τειρομένοις ἑτάροισιν ἀμυνέμεν αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr:
nai dē tauta ge teknon etētymon ou kakon esti
teiromenois hetaroisin amynemen aipyn olethron.
sentences.l:
“Yes indeed, child, this is true: it is not bad
to ward steep destruction away from companions who are worn down.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, child, that is true: it is no bad thing to ward steep destruction away from companions who are worn down.
sentences.n: ναὶ δὴ is ‘yes indeed’, and ταῦτά γε ἐτήτυμον ‘this is true’ grants Achilles’ point before she objects. ἀμυνέμεν is the infinitive of ἀμύνω, here with a dative of the people helped (τειρομένοις ἑτάροισιν) and an accusative of what is warded off. τειρομένοις ‘worn down’ is a participle of τείρω. αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον is ‘steep destruction’, the Odyssey’s rendering, and the sense of αἰπύς, ‘steep’, in such a phrase is disputed.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τοι ἔντεα καλὰ μετὰ Τρώεσσιν ἔχονται
χάλκεα μαρμαίροντα·
sentences.tr:
alla toi entea kala meta Trōessin echontai
chalkea marmaironta·
sentences.l:
But your armour, fine, is held among the Trojans,
bronze, sparkling;
sentences.i: But your fine armour is held among the Trojans, bronze and sparkling;
sentences.n: ἀλλά τοι is ‘but’ with the enclitic τοι, ‘to you’, read here as ‘your’ armour (it may also be the particle ‘mark you’). ἔντεα is ‘armour’, and ἔχονται is the middle of ἔχω used as a passive, ‘are held’. μετά with the dative Τρώεσσιν is ‘among the Trojans’. μαρμαίροντα is a participle of μαρμαίρω ‘flash, sparkle’. The armour is that of Achilles, which Patroclus wore and Hector took from his body.

sentences.t:
τὰ μὲν κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ
αὐτὸς ἔχων ὤμοισιν ἀγάλλεται·
sentences.tr:
ta men korythaiolos Hektōr
autos echōn ōmoisin agalletai·
sentences.l:
those things Hector of the glancing helmet
himself, having them on his shoulders, exults in;
sentences.i: Hector of the glancing helmet himself wears them on his shoulders and exults in them;
sentences.n: τὰ μέν is ‘these’, the arms just mentioned, the object of ἔχων. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s stock epithet, translated every time. ἔχων ὤμοισιν is ‘having on his shoulders’, with the dative ὤμοισιν, and ἀγάλλεται ‘exults’ takes the armour as its cause. Pause at the ano teleia, mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ ἕ φημι
δηρὸν ἐπαγλαϊεῖσθαι, ἐπεὶ φόνος ἐγγύθεν αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
oude he phēmi
dēron epaglaïeisthai, epei phonos engythen autōi.
sentences.l:
and I say that not for long
will he glory in them, since slaughter is near for him.
sentences.i: but I tell you he will not take pride in them for long, since slaughter is close at hand for him.
sentences.n: οὐδέ ἕ φημι with the future infinitive ἐπαγλαϊεῖσθαι is ‘and I say that he will not …’, ἕ being ‘him’ and the negative belonging with the infinitive. ἐπαγλαϊεῖσθαι is the future of ἐπαγλαΐζομαι ‘take pride in’. φόνος is ‘slaughter, killing’, and ἐγγύθεν αὐτῷ ‘near for him’. Thetis can say it because she knows Achilles will kill Hector.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν μή πω καταδύσεο μῶλον Ἄρηος
πρίν γ’ ἐμὲ δεῦρ’ ἐλθοῦσαν ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδηαι·
sentences.tr:
alla sy men mē pō katadyseo mōlon Arēos
prin g’ eme deur’ elthousan en ophthalmoisin idēai·
sentences.l:
But you, do not yet enter the toil of Ares
before you see me, come here, with your eyes;
sentences.i: But you, do not yet enter the toil of battle before you see me here with your own eyes;
sentences.n: μή πω καταδύσεο is a prohibition, ‘do not yet go down into’, from καταδύω; μῶλον Ἄρηος ‘the toil of Ares’ is the fixed phrase for the labour of battle. πρίν γ’ … ἴδηαι is ‘before you see’, an aorist subjunctive in an epic form. ἐμὲ δεῦρ’ ἐλθοῦσαν ‘me, having come here’ is an accusative participle agreeing with ἐμέ. ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is ‘with your eyes’.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν γὰρ νεῦμαι ἅμ’ ἠελίῳ ἀνιόντι
τεύχεα καλὰ φέρουσα παρ’ Ἡφαίστοιο ἄνακτος.
sentences.tr:
ēōthen gar neumai ham’ ēeliōi anionti
teuchea kala pherousa par’ Hēphaistoio anaktos.
sentences.l:
for at dawn I shall return, with the rising sun,
bringing fine armour from lord Hephaestus.”
sentences.i: for at dawn I shall come back with the rising sun, bringing fine armour from lord Hephaestus.”
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν ‘at dawn’ is an adverb in -θεν. νεῦμαι is present in form but means ‘I shall go, return’ and is a form of νέομαι. ἅμ’ ἠελίῳ ἀνιόντι is ‘together with the rising sun’, with the participle in the dative. φέρουσα is ‘bearing’ and παρ’ is παρά with the genitive, ‘from beside’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα πάλιν τράπεθ’ υἷος ἑοῖο,
καὶ στρεφθεῖσ’ ἁλίῃσι κασιγνήτῃσι μετηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsasa palin trapeth’ huios heoio,
kai strephtheis’ haliēisi kasignētēisi metēuda·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken she turned back from her son,
and, having turned to her sisters of the sea, addressed them:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and turned away from her son; then she turned to her sisters of the sea and said:
sentences.n: τράπεθ’ is the aorist middle τράπετο, ‘she turned’, with the final vowel dropped and the τ made θ before the rough breathing of υἷος. στρεφθεῖσ’ is an aorist passive participle, ‘having been turned’. ἁλίῃσι κασιγνήτῃσι is ‘sisters of the sea’, the Nereids, in the dative ending -ῃσι. μετηύδα ‘spoke among’ is an imperfect of μεταυδάω. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς μὲν νῦν δῦτε θαλάσσης εὐρέα κόλπον
ὀψόμεναί τε γέρονθ’ ἅλιον καὶ δώματα πατρός,
καί οἱ πάντ’ ἀγορεύσατ’·
sentences.tr:
hymeis men nyn dyte thalassēs eurea kolpon
opsomenai te geronth’ halion kai dōmata patros,
kai hoi pant’ agoreusat’·
sentences.i: “You, for your part, go down now into the broad bosom of the sea, to see the old man of the sea and our father’s house, and tell him everything;
sentences.n: The speech is to the sisters, so the verbs are plural. δῦτε is an aorist imperative of δύω ‘sink, go down into’, taking the accusative κόλπον ‘bosom, gulf’. ὀψόμεναι is a future participle of purpose, ‘to see’. γέρων ἅλιος is ‘the old man of the sea’, Nereus, father of the Nereids, who is not named. ἀγορεύσατε is an aorist imperative of ἀγορεύω, with the final -ε dropped.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον
εἶμι παρ’ Ἥφαιστον κλυτοτέχνην, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν
υἱεῖ ἐμῷ δόμεναι κλυτὰ τεύχεα παμφανόωντα.
sentences.tr:
egō d’ es makron Olympon
eimi par’ Hēphaiston klytotechnēn, ai k’ ethelēisin
huiei emōi domenai klyta teuchea pamphanoōnta.
sentences.l:
and I to tall Olympus
will go, to Hephaestus, famous in craft, in case he is willing
to give my son famous armour, all-shining.”
sentences.i: and I shall go to tall Olympus, to Hephaestus, famous in craft, in case he is willing to give my son famous, all-shining armour.”
sentences.n: ἐγὼ δέ sets her own errand against theirs. εἶμι is present in form, ‘I shall go’. μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον is ‘tall Olympus’, the mountain of the gods. κλυτοτέχνης is ‘famous in craft’, the stock epithet of Hephaestus, translated every time. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν is ‘in case he is willing’. δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι, ‘to give’, and κλυτά ‘famous’ and παμφανόωντα ‘all-shining’ both agree with τεύχεα.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἳ δ’ ὑπὸ κῦμα θαλάσσης αὐτίκ’ ἔδυσαν·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hai d’ hypo kyma thalassēs autik’ edysan·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and they beneath the wave of the sea at once went down;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and they at once went down beneath the wave of the sea;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so she spoke’, the formula closing a speech. αἳ δ’ is the demonstrative pronoun, ‘they’, that is the Nereids. ἔδυσαν is an aorist of δύω ‘sink, go down’. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ αὖτ’ Οὔλυμπον δὲ θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα
ἤϊεν ὄφρα φίλῳ παιδὶ κλυτὰ τεύχε’ ἐνείκαι.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ aut’ Oulympon de thea Thetis argyropeza
ēïen ophra philōi paidi klyta teuche’ eneikai.
sentences.l:
and she, in turn, to Olympus, the goddess Thetis, silver-footed,
went, so that she might bring her dear son famous armour.
sentences.i: while she, the goddess Thetis, silver-footed, went on to Olympus, to bring her dear son famous armour.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ αὖτ’ ‘and she, for her part’ turns from the sisters to Thetis. Οὔλυμπον δέ is Olympus with the suffix -δε ‘to’, so ‘to Olympus’. ἤϊεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and ὄφρα with ἐνείκαι gives her purpose; ἐνείκαι is the Aeolic aorist optative of φέρω (= ἐνέγκοι), ‘that she might bring’, not the infinitive, which would be accented ἐνεῖκαι. ἀργυρόπεζα ‘silver-footed’ is her stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t: τὴν μὲν ἄρ’ Οὔλυμπον δὲ πόδες φέρον·
sentences.tr: tēn men ar’ Oulympon de podes pheron·
sentences.l: Her, then, to Olympus her feet carried;
sentences.i: So her feet carried her to Olympus;
sentences.n: τὴν is Thetis, ‘her’, and the line ends at the ano teleia after φέρον ‘carried’, an imperfect without the augment. πόδες φέρον is the common way of saying that someone went on foot. Οὔλυμπον δέ is ‘to Olympus’, as in the previous line. The line begins a new paragraph and turns the story back to the fighting.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
θεσπεσίῳ ἀλαλητῷ ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο
φεύγοντες νῆάς τε καὶ Ἑλλήσποντον ἵκοντο.
sentences.tr:
autar Achaioi
thespesiōi alalētōi hyph’ Hektoros androphonoio
pheugontes nēas te kai Hellēsponton hikonto.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans,
with a wondrous shout, under man-slaying Hector,
fleeing, reached the ships and the Hellespont.
sentences.i: while the Achaeans, with a wondrous cry going up and man-slaying Hector driving them, fled and reached the ships and the Hellespont.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ opens the contrast with Thetis. θεσπέσιος is ‘marvellous, uncanny’, and the dative ἀλαλητῷ ‘with a war-cry’ is said without naming who shouts. ὑφ’ Ἕκτορος is ‘under Hector’, that is, pressed by him. ἀνδροφόνοιο ‘man-slaying’ is Hector’s stock epithet. ἵκοντο is an aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive’, and the Hellespont is the strait by whose shore the ships lie.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κε Πάτροκλόν περ ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐκ βελέων ἐρύσαντο νέκυν θεράποντ’ Ἀχιλῆος·
sentences.tr:
oude ke Patroklon per eÿknēmides Achaioi
ek beleōn erysanto nekyn therapont’ Achilēos·
sentences.l:
And not even Patroclus would the well-greaved Achaeans
have drawn out from the missiles, the dead attendant of Achilles;
sentences.i: And the well-greaved Achaeans would not have drawn even Patroclus, the dead attendant of Achilles, out from the missiles;
sentences.n: οὐδέ κε with the aorist ἐρύσαντο is a contrary-to-fact statement about the past, ‘would not have drawn’, and the condition is given at line 166. ἐϋκνήμιδες is ‘well-greaved’, translated every time. ἐκ βελέων is ‘out of the missiles’. νέκυν is ‘corpse’, and θεράποντ’ Ἀχιλῆος ‘Achilles’ attendant’ is added to it. θεράπων is ‘attendant, squire’.

sentences.t:
αὖτις γὰρ δὴ τόν γε κίχον λαός τε καὶ ἵπποι
Ἕκτωρ τε Πριάμοιο πάϊς φλογὶ εἴκελος ἀλκήν.
sentences.tr:
autis gar dē ton ge kichon laos te kai hippoi
Hektōr te Priamoio païs phlogi eikelos alkēn.
sentences.l:
for again they came upon him, the host and the horses
and Hector, Priam’s son, like flame in might.
sentences.i: for the host and the horses, and Hector, son of Priam, like flame in might, caught up with him again.
sentences.n: κίχον is an aorist of κιχάνω, ‘overtake, come upon’, without the augment, and it has three subjects: λαός ‘the host’, ἵπποι ‘horses’ and Ἕκτωρ. τόν is Patroclus’ body, which the Achaeans were carrying off. Πριάμοιο πάϊς is ‘Priam’s son’, and φλογὶ εἴκελος ἀλκήν is ‘like flame in might’, where ἀλκήν is an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μέν μιν μετόπισθε ποδῶν λάβε φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
ἑλκέμεναι μεμαώς, μέγα δὲ Τρώεσσιν ὁμόκλα·
sentences.tr:
tris men min metopisthe podōn labe phaidimos Hektōr
helkemenai memaōs, mega de Trōessin homokla·
sentences.l:
Three times, then, from behind by the feet seized him glorious Hector,
eager to drag, and loudly to the Trojans he shouted;
sentences.i: Three times glorious Hector seized him from behind by the feet, eager to drag him off, and shouted loudly to the Trojans;
sentences.n: τρίς ‘three times’ opens a threefold pattern that continues in the next lines with τρὶς δέ. λάβε is an aorist of λαμβάνω, ‘took hold of’, with the genitive ποδῶν ‘by the feet’; μετόπισθε is ‘from behind’. ἑλκέμεναι is an infinitive, ‘to drag’, after μεμαώς ‘eager’, a perfect participle. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is Hector’s stock epithet, translated every time. ὁμόκλα is an imperfect, ‘kept shouting’.

sentences.t:
τρὶς δὲ δύ’ Αἴαντες θοῦριν ἐπιειμένοι ἀλκὴν
νεκροῦ ἀπεστυφέλιξαν·
sentences.tr:
tris de dy’ Aiantes thourin epieimenoi alkēn
nekrou apestyphelixan·
sentences.l:
and three times the two Ajaxes, clothed in impetuous might,
drove him back from the corpse;
sentences.i: and three times the two Ajaxes, clothed in impetuous might, drove him back from the corpse;
sentences.n: δύ’ Αἴαντες is ‘the two Ajaxes’, that is, the son of Telamon and the son of Oileus, as the plural of a name that has two bearers. ἐπιειμένοι is a perfect passive participle, ‘clothed in’, with the accusative ἀλκήν, ‘might’, and θοῦριν is ‘impetuous’. ἀπεστυφέλιξαν is an aorist of ἀποστυφελίζω, ‘thrust back’, and νεκροῦ is a genitive of separation. Pause at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἔμπεδον ἀλκὶ πεποιθὼς
ἄλλοτ’ ἐπαΐξασκε κατὰ μόθον, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε
στάσκε μέγα ἰάχων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ empedon alki pepoithōs
allot’ epaïxaske kata mothon, allote d’ aute
staske mega iachōn·
sentences.i: but he, trusting steadfastly in his might, would now rush into the press of fighting and now stand still, crying out loudly;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Hector. ἐπαΐξασκε and στάσκε are iterative forms with the ending -σκ-, ‘would leap’, ‘would stand’, which show repeated action. ἔμπεδον is ‘steadfastly’, and ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς is ‘trusting in his might’, a dative with a perfect participle. μόθον is ‘the throng of battle’. μέγα ἰάχων ‘shouting loudly’ takes ἰάχω, which means ‘cry out’. Pause at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ὀπίσω δ’ οὐ χάζετο πάμπαν.
sentences.tr: opisō d’ ou chazeto pampan.
sentences.l: but backward he would not at all draw back.
sentences.i: but he never drew back at all.
sentences.n: οὐ χάζετο πάμπαν is ‘he did not give way at all’. χάζετο is an imperfect of χάζομαι ‘draw back, give ground’, and ὀπίσω is ‘backward’. πάμπαν is an adverb, ‘altogether’, and with οὐ it means ‘not at all’. The line closes the threefold struggle over the body.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ἀπὸ σώματος οὔ τι λέοντ’ αἴθωνα δύνανται
ποιμένες ἄγραυλοι μέγα πεινάοντα δίεσθαι,
ὥς ῥα τὸν οὐκ ἐδύναντο δύω Αἴαντε κορυστὰ
Ἕκτορα Πριαμίδην ἀπὸ νεκροῦ δειδίξασθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ apo sōmatos ou ti leont’ aithōna dynantai
poimenes agrauloi mega peinaonta diesthai,
hōs rha ton ouk edynanto dyō Aiante korysta
Hektora Priamidēn apo nekrou deidixasthai.
sentences.l:
And as from a carcass a tawny lion they cannot drive off,
the field-dwelling herdsmen, when he is greatly hungry,
so the two Ajaxes, armed, were not able
to frighten Hector, Priam’s son, from the corpse.
sentences.i: And as field-dwelling herdsmen cannot drive a tawny lion away from a carcass when he is ravenous, so the two armed Ajaxes could not frighten Hector, son of Priam, away from the corpse.
sentences.n: A simile: ὡς … ὥς ῥα is ‘as … so’. In Homer σῶμα means a dead body, and here a carcass. αἴθων is ‘tawny, fiery’, a word whose colour is not decided. ποιμένες ἄγραυλοι are herdsmen who live out in the fields, and μέγα πεινάοντα is ‘greatly hungering’. δίεσθαι is ‘to drive off’. The dual Αἴαντε κορυστά is ‘the two armed Ajaxes’. δειδίξασθαι is an aorist middle infinitive of δειδίσσομαι, ‘to frighten away’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν εἴρυσσέν τε καὶ ἄσπετον ἤρατο κῦδος,
εἰ μὴ Πηλεΐωνι ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις
ἄγγελος ἦλθε θέουσ’ ἀπ’ Ὀλύμπου θωρήσσεσθαι
κρύβδα Διὸς ἄλλων τε θεῶν·
sentences.tr:
kai ny ken eiryssen te kai aspeton ērato kydos,
ei mē Pēleïōni podēnemos ōkea Iris
angelos ēlthe theous’ ap’ Olympou thōrēssesthai
krybda Dios allōn te theōn·
sentences.l:
And now he would have dragged him off and won boundless glory,
if not to Peleus’ son wind-footed, swift Iris
came as a messenger, running from Olympus, to arm,
secretly from Zeus and the other gods;
sentences.i: And now he would have dragged him off and won boundless glory, had Iris, wind-footed and swift, not come running from Olympus as a messenger to the son of Peleus, to tell him to arm, without the knowledge of Zeus and the other gods;
sentences.n: εἰ μή ‘if not’ with κεν ... εἴρυσσε is a contrary-to-fact clause: Hector would have dragged the body off. Πηλεΐωνι is a patronymic, ‘son of Peleus’, that is, Achilles. Iris is ποδήνεμος ὠκέα, ‘wind-footed, swift’, and ἄγγελος ἦλθε θέουσα ‘came running as a messenger’. θωρήσσεσθαι is the infinitive ‘to arm’. κρύβδα, ‘secretly’ with the genitive, means ‘hidden from’. Lines 165 and 167 also stand in earlier parts, and their English is reused here. Pause at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: πρὸ γὰρ ἧκέ μιν Ἥρη.
sentences.tr: pro gar hēke min Hērē.
sentences.l: for forth had sent her Hera.
sentences.i: for Hera had sent her forth.
sentences.n: πρὸ … ἧκε is tmesis, the prefix πρό standing apart from its verb, for προέηκε ‘sent forth’. ἧκε is an aorist of ἵημι ‘send’. μιν is Iris, ‘her’. The clause explains why Iris came secretly: it was Hera, not Zeus, who sent her.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenē epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words she spoke to him:
sentences.i: Standing close beside him, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: A whole-line speech introduction found many times in the poem; the subject is Iris. ἔπεα πτερόεντα, ‘winged words’, is the usual phrase for words that fly from speaker to hearer, translated every time. ἱσταμένη is a present participle, ‘standing’, and προσηύδα an imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t: ὄρσεο Πηλεΐδη, πάντων ἐκπαγλότατ’ ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr: orseo Pēleïdē, pantōn ekpaglotat’ andrōn·
sentences.l: “Rise up, son of Peleus, most terrifying of all men;
sentences.i: “Rise up, son of Peleus, most terrifying of all men;
sentences.n: ὄρσεο is an aorist middle imperative of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse yourself, rise up’. Πηλεΐδη is a vocative patronymic, ‘son of Peleus’. ἐκπαγλότατ’ is a superlative, ‘most terrifying’, from ἔκπαγλος, with the genitive πάντων ἀνδρῶν ‘of all men’. Iris greets Achilles with the praise she then uses to rouse him.

sentences.t:
Πατρόκλῳ ἐπάμυνον, οὗ εἵνεκα φύλοπις αἰνὴ
ἕστηκε πρὸ νεῶν·
sentences.tr:
Patroklōi epamynon, hou heineka phylopis ainē
hestēke pro neōn·
sentences.l:
come to the defence of Patroclus, for whose sake the fearsome din of battle
stands before the ships;
sentences.i: come to the defence of Patroclus, for whose sake the fearsome din of battle stands before the ships;
sentences.n: ἐπάμυνον is an imperative of ἐπαμύνω, ‘come to the defence of’, with the dative Πατρόκλῳ. οὗ εἵνεκα is ‘for whose sake’, the οὗ being the relative of Patroclus. φύλοπις αἰνή is ‘the fearsome din of battle’, and ἕστηκε is the perfect of ἵστημι, which has the sense of the present, ‘stands’. Pause at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀλλήλους ὀλέκουσιν
οἳ μὲν ἀμυνόμενοι νέκυος πέρι τεθνηῶτος,
οἳ δὲ ἐρύσσασθαι ποτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν
Τρῶες ἐπιθύουσι·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ allēlous olekousin
hoi men amynomenoi nekyos peri tethnēōtos,
hoi de eryssasthai poti Ilion ēnemoessan
Trōes epithyousi·
sentences.l:
and they are destroying one another,
the one side defending themselves around the dead body,
the others, to drag him off to windy Ilios,
the Trojans, are rushing on;
sentences.i: and they are killing one another, the one side defending themselves around the dead body, the others, the Trojans, rushing on to drag him off to windy Ilios;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘they’, both sides, and then οἳ μέν … οἳ δέ divides them: one side defends, the other attacks. ὀλέκουσιν is ‘destroy, kill’. νέκυος … τεθνηῶτος is ‘around the dead corpse’, with περί after the noun, and τεθνηῶτος a perfect participle of θνήσκω. ἐρύσσασθαι is an aorist middle infinitive, ‘to drag off’. Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν, ‘windy Ilios’, is the stock epithet of Troy, translated every time.

sentences.t:
μάλιστα δὲ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
ἑλκέμεναι μέμονεν·
sentences.tr:
malista de phaidimos Hektōr
helkemenai memonen·
sentences.l:
and most of all glorious Hector
is eager to drag him;
sentences.i: and most of all glorious Hector is set on dragging him off;
sentences.n: μάλιστα δέ is ‘and most of all’. μέμονεν is a perfect with present sense, ‘is eager, is bent on’, and ἑλκέμεναι is the infinitive of ἕλκω ‘drag’. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is Hector’s stock epithet. Pause at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κεφαλὴν δέ ἑ θυμὸς ἄνωγε
πῆξαι ἀνὰ σκολόπεσσι ταμόνθ’ ἁπαλῆς ἀπὸ δειρῆς.
sentences.tr:
kephalēn de he thymos anōge
pēxai ana skolopessi tamonth’ hapalēs apo deirēs.
sentences.l:
and his heart bids him
fix the head on stakes, cutting it from the tender neck.
sentences.i: and his heart bids him cut the head from the tender neck and fix it on stakes.
sentences.n: The object κεφαλήν is placed first, with ἑ ‘him’ meaning Hector. ἄνωγε is a perfect with present sense, ‘bids, urges’, and takes the infinitive πῆξαι ‘to fix’, an aorist of πήγνυμι. σκολόπεσσι is a dative plural of σκόλοψ, ‘pointed stake’, and ταμόντα is an aorist participle of τέμνω ‘cut’ with its final vowel dropped before ἁπαλῆς. The mutilation of a corpse is what the next lines call λώβη, outrage.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄνα μηδ’ ἔτι κεῖσο·
sentences.tr: all’ ana mēd’ eti keiso·
sentences.l: But up! No longer lie there;
sentences.i: But get up! Lie there no longer;
sentences.n: ἄνα is the short form of ἀνάστηθι ‘get up!’. μηδ’ ἔτι κεῖσο is a prohibition, ‘no longer lie’, with κεῖσο the imperative of κεῖμαι (the same verb as κείσομ’ at line 121). Achilles has done nothing since the news but lie in grief.

sentences.t:
σέβας δέ σε θυμὸν ἱκέσθω
Πάτροκλον Τρῳῇσι κυσὶν μέλπηθρα γενέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
sebas de se thymon hikesthō
Patroklon Trōiēisi kysin melpēthra genesthai·
sentences.l:
let awe come upon you in your heart
that Patroclus become playthings for Trojan dogs;
sentences.i: let awe come upon you in your heart that Patroclus should become the playthings of Trojan dogs;
sentences.n: σέβας is ‘awe’, and here the awe that holds a man back from a shameful thing. ἱκέσθω is the aorist imperative of ἱκνέομαι, ‘let it reach’. σε θυμόν is ‘you, in your heart’, both accusatives. The infinitive γενέσθαι ‘become’ gives what the awe is about. μέλπηθρα ‘playthings’ is plural, and Τρῳῇσι κυσίν ‘Trojan dogs’ is a dative of the one for whom. The last line is repeated elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t: σοὶ λώβη, αἴ κέν τι νέκυς ᾐσχυμμένος ἔλθῃ.
sentences.tr: soi lōbē, ai ken ti nekys ēischymmenos elthēi.
sentences.l: to you the outrage, if the corpse should come in any way disfigured.”
sentences.i: The outrage will be yours if the corpse comes disfigured in any way.”
sentences.n: σοὶ λώβη has no verb: ‘to you (belongs) the outrage’. λώβη is ‘outrage, shameful treatment’. αἴ κέν … ἔλθῃ is ‘if … should come’, an aorist subjunctive with κέν, and τι ‘in any way’ is adverbial. ᾐσχυμμένος is a perfect passive participle of αἰσχύνω ‘disfigure, shame’. Iris’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita podarkēs dios Achilleus·
sentences.l: Her then answered swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Then swift-footed, heavenly Achilles answered her:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula. τὴν is Iris, ‘her’. ποδάρκης ‘swift-footed’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are Achilles’ stock epithets here and are translated every time; ποδάρκης is kept apart from πόδας ὠκύς, ‘swift in feet’. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t: Ἶρι θεὰ τίς γάρ σε θεῶν ἐμοὶ ἄγγελον ἧκε;
sentences.tr: Iri thea tis gar se theōn emoi angelon hēke;
sentences.l: “Iris, goddess, which of the gods has sent you to me as a messenger?”
sentences.i: “Goddess Iris, which of the gods has sent you to me as a messenger?”
sentences.n: Ἶρι θεά is a vocative, ‘Iris, goddess’. τίς … θεῶν is ‘which of the gods’, a question with the genitive. ἧκε is an aorist of ἵημι ‘send’, and ἄγγελον is the predicate, ‘as a messenger’. He asks because the one who sent her would be the god who wants him to fight. Achilles does not yet know the answer, which is given next.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe podēnemos ōkea Iris·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed wind-footed, swift Iris:
sentences.i: Then Iris, wind-footed and swift, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula with αὖτε ‘in turn’; the speaker is Iris, and the same line opens her second speech at line 196. ποδήνεμος ‘wind-footed’ and ὠκέα ‘swift’ are her stock epithets, translated every time. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t: Ἥρη με προέηκε Διὸς κυδρὴ παράκοιτις·
sentences.tr: Hērē me proeēke Dios kydrē parakoitis·
sentences.l: “Hera sent me forth, the glorious consort of Zeus;
sentences.i: “Hera sent me forth, the glorious consort of Zeus;
sentences.n: προέηκε is an aorist of προίημι ‘send forth’, with the prefix attached, unlike line 168. κυδρή is ‘glorious’, from κῦδος ‘glory’, as in the Odyssey’s Διὸς κυδρὴν παράκοιτιν. παράκοιτις ‘consort’ is a wife, literally one who lies beside. Zeus is in the genitive, Διός.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ οἶδε Κρονίδης ὑψίζυγος οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
ἀθανάτων, οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἀγάννιφον ἀμφινέμονται.
sentences.tr:
oud’ oide Kronidēs hypsizygos oude tis allos
athanatōn, hoi Olympon aganniphon amphinemontai.
sentences.l:
and the son of Cronus, sitting on high, does not know, nor does any other
of the immortals, who dwell around snowy Olympus.”
sentences.i: and neither Zeus, the son of Cronus, who sits on high, nor any other of the immortals who dwell around snowy Olympus knows it.”
sentences.n: οὐδ’ οἶδε … οὐδέ τις ἄλλος is ‘and he does not know, nor does any other’. Κρονίδης ὑψίζυγος is ‘the son of Cronus, who sits on high’, a stock phrase for Zeus, translated every time. ἀγάννιφον is ‘snowy’, and ἀμφινέμονται is ‘dwell around’, a present middle of ἀμφινέμομαι. Iris repeats that she came secretly, as stated at line 168.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to her:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula, the same as at 1.84 and 1.215, so the English is the same. τὴν is Iris. ἀπαμειβόμενος is a present participle, ‘answering’, and προσέφη an aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. πόδας ὠκύς, ‘swift in feet’, is translated every time. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t: πῶς τὰρ ἴω μετὰ μῶλον;
sentences.tr: pōs tar iō meta mōlon;
sentences.l: “How then am I to go among the toil?
sentences.i: “How am I to go into the toil of battle?
sentences.n: The question puts the obstacle plainly. τὰρ, printed as one word, carries the sense ‘then’. ἴω is a subjunctive of εἶμι ‘go’ in a deliberative question, ‘how am I to go?’ μετά with the accusative μῶλον is ‘into the midst of’. Ἄρηος is not said here, so l has only ‘the toil’; μῶλος is the word of Thetis’ μῶλον Ἄρηος at line 134, and i spells it out as ‘the toil of battle’.

sentences.t: ἔχουσι δὲ τεύχε’ ἐκεῖνοι·
sentences.tr: echousi de teuche’ ekeinoi·
sentences.l: and they have armour, those men;
sentences.i: for those men have my armour;
sentences.n: ἔχουσι is ‘they hold’, and ἐκεῖνοι ‘those men’, the Trojans, is put last for emphasis. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’ with the final vowel dropped. The armour is Achilles’ own, which Patroclus had worn and Hector took.

sentences.t:
μήτηρ δ’ οὔ με φίλη πρίν γ’ εἴα θωρήσσεσθαι
πρίν γ’ αὐτὴν ἐλθοῦσαν ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδωμαι·
sentences.tr:
mētēr d’ ou me philē prin g’ eia thōrēssesthai
prin g’ autēn elthousan en ophthalmoisin idōmai·
sentences.l:
and my dear mother did not allow me to arm myself
before I see her herself, having come, with my eyes;
sentences.i: and my dear mother would not let me arm myself until I see her come with my own eyes;
sentences.n: εἴα is the imperfect of ἐάω, ‘she allowed’, so οὔ … εἴα is ‘she did not allow’. θωρήσσεσθαι is the infinitive ‘to arm oneself’. πρίν γ’ … ἴδωμαι is ‘before I see’, an aorist subjunctive, with the accusative αὐτὴν ἐλθοῦσαν ‘her herself having come’. This repeats what Thetis said at lines 134–135.

sentences.t: στεῦτο γὰρ Ἡφαίστοιο πάρ’ οἰσέμεν ἔντεα καλά.
sentences.tr: steuto gar Hēphaistoio par’ oisemen entea kala.
sentences.l: for she vowed to bring from Hephaestus fine armour.
sentences.i: for she promised to bring me fine armour from Hephaestus.
sentences.n: στεῦτο is an imperfect of a rare verb meaning ‘vow, promise’ or ‘threaten’, here ‘vowed’. οἰσέμεν is an infinitive of φέρω, ‘to bring’, built on the stem of the future οἴσω. Ἡφαίστοιο πάρ’ is ‘from Hephaestus’, with πάρ’ placed after its noun and meaning παρά ‘from beside’. ἔντεα καλά is ‘fine armour’, and the phrase has the same words as line 130.

sentences.t:
ἄλλου δ’ οὔ τευ οἶδα τεῦ ἂν κλυτὰ τεύχεα δύω,
εἰ μὴ Αἴαντός γε σάκος Τελαμωνιάδαο.
sentences.tr:
allou d’ ou teu oida teu an klyta teuchea dyō,
ei mē Aiantos ge sakos Telamōniadao.
sentences.l:
And of no other do I know whose famous armour I could put on,
unless it is the shield of Ajax, son of Telamon.
sentences.i: And I know of no one else whose famous armour I could put on, unless it is the shield of Ajax, son of Telamon.
sentences.n: οὔ τευ οἶδα is ‘I know of no one’, where τευ is the epic form of τινός ‘anyone’ and τεῦ in the next words is that of τίνος ‘whose?’. ἂν … δύω is an aorist subjunctive with ἄν, ‘whose armour I might put on’. κλυτά ‘famous’ goes with τεύχεα ‘armour’. εἰ μή is ‘except’. Τελαμωνιάδαο is a patronymic, ‘son of Telamon’, in the genitive -άο.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς ὅ γ’ ἔλπομ’ ἐνὶ πρώτοισιν ὁμιλεῖ
ἔγχεϊ δηϊόων περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος.
sentences.tr:
alla kai autos ho g’ elpom’ eni prōtoisin homilei
encheï dēïoōn peri Patrokloio thanontos.
sentences.l:
But he himself too, I expect, is in the throng among the foremost,
with his spear cutting down, around dead Patroclus.”
sentences.i: But he himself too, I expect, is in the throng among the foremost, cutting men down with his spear over the dead Patroclus.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτός opens a second hope: Ajax himself, ‘too’, is fighting. ἔλπομαι is ‘I expect, I hope’. ὁμιλεῖ is ‘is in the throng’, and ἐνὶ πρώτοισιν is ‘among the foremost’. δηϊόων is a participle of δηϊόω, ‘cut down’, with the dative ἔγχεϊ ‘with his spear’. περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος is ‘around the dead Patroclus’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe podēnemos ōkea Iris·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed wind-footed, swift Iris:
sentences.i: Then Iris, wind-footed and swift, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at line 183, so the English is the same. The speaker is Iris and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks her second speech. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t: εὖ νυ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἴδμεν ὅ τοι κλυτὰ τεύχε’ ἔχονται·
sentences.tr: eu ny kai hēmeis idmen ho toi klyta teuche’ echontai·
sentences.l: “Well indeed we too know that your famous armour is held;
sentences.i: “We know well enough that your famous armour is held by them;
sentences.n: εὖ νυ is ‘well, now’, and ἴδμεν is the epic form of ἴσμεν, ‘we know’, in the plural; Iris includes herself with the gods. ὅ is the neuter relative used as ‘that’. τοι is ‘to you’, and κλυτὰ τεύχε’ ἔχονται, ‘famous armour is held’, echoes lines 130 and 131.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αὔτως ἐπὶ τάφρον ἰὼν Τρώεσσι φάνηθι,
αἴ κέ σ’ ὑποδείσαντες ἀπόσχωνται πολέμοιο
Τρῶες, ἀναπνεύσωσι δ’ ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
τειρόμενοι· ὀλίγη δέ τ’ ἀνάπνευσις πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
all’ autōs epi taphron iōn Trōessi phanēthi,
ai ke s’ hypodeisantes aposchōntai polemoio
Trōes, anapneusōsi d’ arēïoi huies Achaiōn
teiromenoi· oligē de t’ anapneusis polemoio.
sentences.l:
But as you are, go to the ditch and show yourself to the Trojans,
in case, fearing you, they may hold off from the war,
the Trojans, and the warlike sons of the Achaeans may get breath again,
worn down; and small is the breathing-space from war.”
sentences.i: But go to the ditch just as you are and show yourself to the Trojans, in case they take fright at you and hold back from war, and the warlike sons of the Achaeans, worn down, get their breath back; and the breathing-space from war is small.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ αὔτως is ‘just as you are’, that is, unarmed. ἐπὶ τάφρον ἰών is ‘going to the ditch’, the trench dug before the Achaean wall. ὑποδείσαντες is an aorist participle, ‘having become afraid’ of him, and ἀπόσχωνται ‘hold off’ and ἀναπνεύσωσι ‘get breath again’ are aorist subjunctives after αἴ κε. ἀρήϊοι is ‘warlike’, and τειρόμενοι ‘worn down’. The final clause, with its general-truth τε, says that a pause in war is short.
